body:
### Problem

`:restart!` uses Nvim's current directory at the time of `:restart` instead of the one used during initial start (i.e. shell's directory). This can cause problems if Nvim is started with relative path as an argument.

### Steps to reproduce

1. From the root of this repo start `nvim --clean LICENSE.txt`. It opens `LICENSE.txt` as expected.
2. `:cd src`
3. `:restart!` - there is an empty buffer for `LICENSE.txt` and `:pwd` shows `path/to/repo/src`.

### Expected behavior

`:restart!` always uses initial current directory when restarting. Or at least `:restart!` with relative path arguments resolves them relative to the initial working directory.

### Nvim version (nvim -v)

NVIM v0.13.0-dev-255+g61daad3bba

### Vim (not Nvim) behaves the same?

No, doesn't have this functionality

### Operating system/version

EndeavourOS Linux x86_64, 6.19.11-arch1-1

### Terminal name/version

Ghostty 1.3.1-arch2

### $TERM environment variable

xterm-ghostty

### Installation

Appimage

comment_data.body: We should handle CWD better, but as a first step, we should go ahead and drop all `[files]` (`v:argf`), similar to how we drop `-- [files]`.

> To drop the `[files]` in `ex_restart()`

of course it's possible to hack it in, but this is beginning to duplicate the parsing done by `command_line_scan` https://github.com/neovim/neovim/blob/a6ea3a1055a374df36cb037ec548698cd9f56fbd/src/nvim/main.c#L1105

so it probably makes sense to think about how to leverage that instead.

I got your concern, if there's new options need value next to it, we have to modify twice in my case. To leverage `command_line_scan`, the same logical we share is that we want to mark the options need next value,

so maybe extract  `bool is_opt_with_value(const char*)`, inside is a `switch case` or `char*[]`, and let it be the only truth. Once we wanna add new argument just add it here.  Replace the `want_argument = true` with it, and some adjust about `argv_idx=xxx`

This is causing unexpected behavior with dir.lua after the new bcd changes.

Reproduce:
1. Open nvim
2. Use dir.lua to navigate to a directory different than the one you started in
3. Type `:restart!`
4. You will now restart into the new directory. The current directory for all scopes (not just buffer) are also set to this directory.

What's the status on #39586 ?

> What's the status on [#39586](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/39586) ?

it adds 2 new globals, hoping there is a better approach

> What's the status on https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/39586 ?

Sorry for blocking the progress of it. It's been a while I haven't work on it because there's no more review from maintainer.

> it adds 2 new globals, hoping there is a better approach

Yes, that's the point. The key is that, `initial_dir` and `argv_is_file` is the context need to live for entire process lifetime. So we need sth like globals to pass this context.

I take your word to mean:

- using static globals and an API to access it.
- reuse the variables that store the global context, like `vimvars`
- sth breaking? e.g.  reorder the `file` params when store args (I don't think this is what you meant.)

@justinmk looking forward to your suggestion:)
i don't have a suggestion, there are 300 PRs open, i need you to find a good solution, else i might as well do it myself.

Hmm, I just want you to take a look at the solution I provide,

> it adds 2 new globals, hoping there is a better approach

and you can just leave this comment in the PR so i can keep on improving it. 
Sorry for the interruption.

> reuse the variables that store the global context, like `vimvars`

If there's something we can reuse, that's preferrable. ideally, we should avoid introducing new state.

passing a parameter somewhere is also fine.

> ideally, we should avoid introducing new state.

Well, I think in this situation, introducing new state is essential.

## `inital_dir`
  It's just the state we need to preserve at the startup if we want to access it later. Once ':cd' is called, we can't access it anymore.

## 'argv_is_file'
  This is the most annoying point. 
> so it probably makes sense to think about how to leverage that instead.

 `command_line_scan`  really do the parse work but no context is left so unless we keep the state, we have no idea to tell if `argv[i]` is `[file]` since we don't want to dup the logic. Also, `command_line_scan` is a giant function that touch so many globals, it can't be reuse anywhere.

### Why don't reuse the current state related to `argv`

- `v:argv` just the copy of `char** argv`.
- `v:argf` it is expand to the absolute path.
- `global_alist` it can be modified using `:argadd` `:argdel`

### Some possible way not to introduce `argv_is_file`?
| Methods | Trade off |
|--------|--------|
| invent or improve the current system, make a reusable `argv parse` | non-trivial  | 
| add a new flag in `argv` that ignore `[files]`| Breaking, introduce new argv| 
| Move `[file]` after `--` when handle `argv`, so it can be easily droped using 1 line code| Changes the observable v:argv|

> passing a parameter somewhere is also fine.

If by “somewhere” you mean passing the information through an existing lifetime/context, I don't see an existing context that survives the point where this information is needed. So the state still needs to be preserved somewhere.

## Conclusion 
Given the above, I currently think preserving these two pieces of state is the simplest approach. I'd like to hear your thoughts. If disagree, which alternative you'd prefer.
Hoping i don't miss any critical context.

I want to point out an improvement that I think could be made with a low code cost.

If we called `vim.fn.getcwd(-1, -1, -1)` (or whatever the C equivalent is) and used that as the directory for the restart, it would at least prevent buffer/win/tab CWD from being used for the restart (and subsequently solve [this](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/39239#issuecomment-5224838785)). It wouldn't solve dropping the file args or changing the global CWD with `:cd` though.

Since https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41304 , the restarted Nvim will gain the global CWD which may have changed after startup. That actually seems like the desired/intuitive behavior. And if so, then the only remaining work to do is to either (1) drop all `[file]` args, or (2) force them to absolute paths in the initial startup, so that they don't depend on the initial CWD.

Does this make sense or where is it wrong?

> Since [#41304](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/41304) , the restarted Nvim will gain the global CWD which may have changed after startup. That actually seems like the desired/intuitive behavior.

To me personally the intuitive behavior is that `:restart!` is equivalent to the "Exit Nvim and execute the previous command to start Nvim". So in this case the cwd after `:restart!` should always be the one that is set in the caller shell. This doesn't seem to be the case on the current `master` (i.e. after #41304).

Also, for preserving cwd there is `:restart` now.

> And if so, then the only remaining work to do is to either (1) drop all `[file]` args, or (2) force them to absolute paths in the initial startup, so that they don't depend on the initial CWD.

Either one would indeed solve the problematic use case of relative file arguments. The exact behavior of what cwd to use after `:restart!` would then be probably more a question of taste, I guess.

> "the cwd after :restart! should always be the one that is set in the caller shell

Personally, i prefer this. With this, we don't even need to handle the `[file]` argv, do we? Currently, we handle the `argv` that conflict with semantic `restart`, like `-S scriptfile`, `--listen server_addr`..., for the `[file]` we only drop `--`, but there are more options that take `[file]` after it, like `-u [file]` `-i [shada]`..., which we don't handle them currently.

> (1) drop all [file] args, or (2) force them to absolute paths in the initial startup, so that they don't depend on the initial CWD.

If they really matter and we want to drop them in the future, (1) look duplicate the logic, (2) of course can solve the problem, but I think, if we use the dir of shell, we don't need to handle the relative path anymore? since it is user's responsibility to make sure the startup context stay unchanged between the two same command.
